name: Water
description: The simplest and most essential compound for life, a bent triatomic molecule with strong hydrogen bonding.
uses: Universal solvent, biological medium, industrial coolant.
interesting_facts: Water is one of the few substances whose solid form (ice) is less dense than its liquid form, which is why ice floats — critical for aquatic life in freezing climates.
bonding_notes: Oxygen's two lone pairs and two O-H bonds occupy a tetrahedral electron arrangement, but only the two bonded pairs define the molecular shape, giving a bond angle of about 104.5°.

name: Methane
description: Simplest alkane hydrocarbon with a perfect tetrahedral geometry, the main component of natural gas.
uses: Fuel source, industrial feedstock for hydrogen and methanol production.
interesting_facts: Methane is the main component of natural gas and a far more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 over a 20-year window, though it breaks down in the atmosphere much faster.
bonding_notes: Four equivalent C-H sigma bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, each separated by the ideal 109.5° angle.

name: Carbon Dioxide
description: A linear triatomic molecule produced by respiration and combustion; a major greenhouse gas.
uses: Photosynthesis feedstock, carbonation in beverages, fire suppression, dry ice.
interesting_facts: Despite each C=O bond being polar, CO2's linear symmetric shape cancels the bond dipoles, making the overall molecule nonpolar.
bonding_notes: Carbon forms two sigma bonds and two pi bonds (one to each oxygen), locking the molecule into a rigid linear O=C=O arrangement.

name: Ammonia
description: A pyramidal molecule with a lone pair on nitrogen, giving it basic and nucleophilic character.
uses: Fertilizer production (Haber process), cleaning agents, refrigerant.
interesting_facts: Ammonia is produced at massive industrial scale via the Haber-Bosch process, underpinning most of the world's synthetic fertilizer supply.
bonding_notes: Nitrogen's lone pair occupies one tetrahedral position, pushing the three N-H bonds into a pyramidal shape with angles of about 107°, slightly less than the ideal 109.5°.

name: Ethanol
description: A simple alcohol with a polar hydroxyl group, produced by fermentation of sugars.
uses: Alcoholic beverages, solvent, antiseptic, biofuel.
interesting_facts: Ethanol is the only alcohol safe for human consumption at beverage concentrations, and is also widely blended into gasoline as a renewable fuel additive.
hybridization: sp3 at both carbons and oxygen
bonding_notes: A tetrahedral CH3 and CH2 carbon connect to a bent, sp3-hybridized hydroxyl oxygen.

name: Acetic Acid
description: A carboxylic acid responsible for the sour taste and smell of vinegar.
uses: Food preservative, industrial solvent, precursor to acetate esters.
interesting_facts: Acetic acid is the main component of vinegar (typically 4-8% by volume) and gives it its characteristic sour taste and sharp smell.
geometry: Trigonal planar at the carboxyl carbon
bonding_notes: The carboxyl carbon is sp2 hybridized; once the acidic proton is lost, resonance delocalizes the negative charge evenly across both oxygens.

name: Glucose
description: A six-carbon monosaccharide that is the primary energy source for living cells.
uses: Cellular respiration fuel, food industry sweetener, IV fluids.
interesting_facts: Glucose is the primary energy source for most living cells — it's the sugar your body breaks down from the carbohydrates you eat.
hybridization: sp3 at the chain carbons, sp2 at the aldehyde carbon in the open-chain form
bonding_notes: In solution, glucose exists mostly as a cyclic hemiacetal (a six-membered pyranose ring), formed when the aldehyde reacts with a hydroxyl group five carbons away.

name: Aspirin
description: A widely used NSAID that inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes to relieve pain and inflammation.
uses: Pain relief, fever reduction, anti-inflammatory, blood clot prevention.
interesting_facts: Aspirin was one of the first drugs sold in pill form and remains one of the most widely used medications in the world, valued for pain relief, anti-inflammatory, and blood-thinning effects.
geometry: Trigonal planar at the aromatic ring and carbonyl carbons
hybridization: sp2 throughout the ring and both carbonyl carbons
bonding_notes: Aspirin combines an aromatic ring with both an ester group and a carboxylic acid group, each contributing sp2 planar character.

name: Caffeine
description: A purine alkaloid and central nervous system stimulant found in coffee, tea, and cacao.
uses: Stimulant in beverages, mild analgesic adjuvant, alertness aid.
interesting_facts: Caffeine is the most widely consumed psychoactive substance in the world, found naturally in coffee, tea, and cacao.
bonding_notes: Caffeine's fused five- and six-membered rings are largely planar, completed by three methyl groups and two carbonyl groups.

name: Benzene
description: The archetypal aromatic hydrocarbon with a delocalized pi-electron ring giving it special stability.
uses: Industrial solvent, precursor to plastics, resins, and synthetic fibers.
interesting_facts: Benzene's true structure — six carbons with electrons spread evenly around the ring — puzzled chemists for decades before resonance theory explained why it doesn't behave like a normal triene.
bonding_notes: Each carbon contributes one electron to a delocalized pi system spanning all six carbons, making every C-C bond equivalent rather than alternating single and double.

name: Glycine
description: The simplest amino acid, achiral, and a building block of proteins and neurotransmitter.
uses: Protein synthesis, dietary supplement, neurotransmitter in the CNS.
interesting_facts: Glycine is the simplest of the 20 standard amino acids and the only one that isn't chiral, since its side chain is just a hydrogen atom.
hybridization: sp3 at the alpha carbon, sp2 at the carboxyl carbon
bonding_notes: The alpha carbon bears an amino group, a carboxylic acid group, and two hydrogens rather than a distinct side chain — which is exactly what makes it non-chiral.

name: Sodium Chloride
description: An ionic compound formed from sodium and chloride ions arranged in a crystal lattice.
uses: Food seasoning and preservation, de-icing roads, chemical industry feedstock.
interesting_facts: Table salt is held together by ionic bonds, not covalent ones — in the solid state it forms a repeating cubic lattice of alternating Na+ and Cl- ions rather than discrete molecules.
geometry: Not molecular; forms a cubic (rock-salt) crystal lattice
hybridization: Not applicable — ionic bonding, no hybridized covalent bonds
bonding_notes: Each Na+ ion is surrounded by six Cl- ions and vice versa. The single bond shown here is a simplification for drawing purposes — real NaCl has no discrete molecules.

name: Sulfuric Acid
description: A highly corrosive strong mineral acid, one of the most produced industrial chemicals.
uses: Fertilizer manufacturing, battery acid, industrial chemical synthesis.
interesting_facts: Sulfuric acid is produced in greater quantity than any other industrial chemical worldwide, used heavily in fertilizer production.
bonding_notes: Sulfur sits at the center of a tetrahedral arrangement of two hydroxyl oxygens and two double-bonded oxygens.

name: Ibuprofen
description: A propionic acid derivative NSAID used to reduce pain, fever, and inflammation.
uses: Pain relief, anti-inflammatory, fever reducer.
interesting_facts: Ibuprofen was discovered in the 1960s and became one of the first widely available over-the-counter NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).
geometry: Trigonal planar at the ring and carboxyl carbon
hybridization: sp2 at the ring and carboxyl carbon, sp3 at the alkyl carbons
bonding_notes: An aromatic ring is flanked by a branched isobutyl group on one side and a propanoic acid group on the other.

name: Methanol
description: The simplest alcohol, toxic to humans, used mainly as an industrial solvent and fuel.
uses: Antifreeze, solvent, fuel additive, formaldehyde production.
interesting_facts: Methanol is toxic to humans in ways ethanol is not, because the body metabolizes it into formaldehyde and formic acid, which can cause blindness or death even in small quantities.
bonding_notes: The simplest alcohol: a tetrahedral carbon bonded to three hydrogens and a hydroxyl group.

name: Ethylene
description: The simplest alkene, featuring a planar carbon-carbon double bond, key plant hormone.
uses: Plastic (polyethylene) production, fruit ripening agent.
interesting_facts: Ethylene is a plant hormone that triggers fruit ripening, and is also the single most-produced organic compound in the chemical industry, used to make polyethylene plastic.
bonding_notes: The C=C double bond consists of one sigma and one pi bond, locking the whole molecule flat and preventing rotation around that bond.

name: Urea
description: The primary nitrogen-containing waste product of protein metabolism in mammals.
uses: Nitrogen fertilizer, resin manufacturing, diuretic in medicine.
interesting_facts: Urea was the first organic compound ever synthesized from inorganic starting materials — a landmark 1828 discovery by Friedrich Wöhler that helped dismantle the idea that organic compounds required a 'vital force' to form.
geometry: Trigonal planar at the carbonyl carbon
bonding_notes: A single carbonyl carbon is flanked by two amine groups — a common motif in how mammals excrete excess nitrogen.

name: Nitric Acid
description: A strong, highly corrosive mineral acid and powerful oxidizing agent.
uses: Fertilizer manufacturing, explosives production, metal etching.
interesting_facts: Nitric acid is a key ingredient in producing ammonium nitrate fertilizer and, historically, various explosives.
bonding_notes: Resonance delocalizes double-bond character across the two non-hydroxyl oxygens, similar to the nitrate ion once the acidic proton is removed.

name: Formaldehyde
description: The simplest aldehyde, a reactive planar molecule used widely in industry.
uses: Preservative, resin/plastic manufacturing, disinfectant.
interesting_facts: Formaldehyde is used as a preservative and disinfectant (as formalin, a water solution) and is also produced in trace amounts naturally within living cells.
bonding_notes: The simplest aldehyde: a planar carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to two hydrogens.

name: Hydrogen Peroxide
description: A simple peroxide with a non-planar, twisted structure and strong oxidizing power.
uses: Disinfectant, bleaching agent, rocket propellant oxidizer.
interesting_facts: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes into water and oxygen gas on contact with catalase, an enzyme abundant in blood and damaged tissue — the fizzing you see on a cut is that reaction happening in real time.
geometry: Bent, non-planar ('open book') around the O-O bond
bonding_notes: The two O-H groups twist out of plane relative to each other around the central O-O single bond, giving an open 'book' shape rather than a flat one.

name: Diethyl Ether
description: A classic laboratory solvent — two ethyl groups joined by an oxygen, with no O-H bond of its own.
uses: Common organic solvent for extractions and reactions; historically used as an early general anesthetic.
interesting_facts: Diethyl ether was one of the first general anesthetics used in surgery, starting in the 1840s, before safer alternatives replaced it. It's also extremely volatile and flammable, so it's rarely used as an anesthetic today.
hybridization: sp3 at oxygen and all four carbons
bonding_notes: The ether oxygen bonds to two carbon chains with no hydrogen of its own, distinguishing it structurally from an alcohol despite having the same formula pattern as some isomers.

name: Sodium Hydroxide
description: A strong base made of sodium and hydroxide ions, drawn here connected for simplicity even though the real substance is ionic.
uses: Soap and paper manufacturing, drain cleaners, food processing (e.g. pretzel and olive curing).
interesting_facts: Solid sodium hydroxide is hygroscopic — it readily absorbs moisture from air — and dissolving it in water is strongly exothermic, releasing enough heat to boil the water if concentrated enough.
geometry: Not molecular in the solid or dissolved state; shown here as a simplified Na-O-H connection
hybridization: Not applicable — this is fundamentally ionic bonding (Na+ and OH-), not covalent
bonding_notes: In reality, NaOH consists of separate Na+ and OH- ions, most often in a crystal lattice (solid) or fully dissociated in water. The bond drawn here between Na and O is a simplification for the sake of visualizing the formula as a connected structure.

name: Polyethylene
description: Shown here as a short six-carbon backbone segment illustrating polyethylene's repeating -CH2-CH2- motif. Real polyethylene chains contain many thousands of repeat units linked end to end — this structure and its formula represent only the illustrative segment, not a full polymer chain.
uses: The world's most widely produced plastic — used in packaging, bottles, bags, and pipes.
interesting_facts: Polyethylene is the most common plastic in the world by production volume, made by joining thousands of ethylene (ethene) molecules into one long carbon-chain polymer.
bonding_notes: Each backbone carbon is sp3 hybridized and singly bonded to its neighbors, the same local geometry repeated thousands of times to build up the full polymer chain — only a short illustrative segment is drawn here.
